summaries.demographer: Irene Tangarife is a 76-year-old divorced Salvadoran American Latina woman living alone in Houston, TX 77083, with grown children and grandchildren nearby or within the broader Houston area (Q05, Q11, Q84, Q88). She was born in Houston to Salvadoran immigrant parents, grew up in a bilingual Spanish-English household, and completed high school plus early childhood credentials rather than a college degree (Q01, Q86, Q90). Her life course reflects working-class immigrant family origins, long-term female caregiving labor, homeownership with a small remaining mortgage, and late-life part-time employment combined with Social Security (Q58, Q72, Q74, Q100-Q107). She remains socially embedded through family, church, teaching networks, and community center activities while preferring a small, familiar circle (Q06, Q07, Q47).
summaries.behavioral_economist: Irene shows strong loss aversion and precautionary budgeting shaped by divorce, modest earnings, aging, and homeownership responsibilities (Q02, Q61, Q83). She favors routines, lists, pantry stocking, early voting, and planned savings as tools for reducing uncertainty, though she admits to worry and occasional disorganization (Q17, Q23, Q50, Q61). Her spending reflects identity and obligation: she protects food, medicine, family meals, church giving, and grandchildren while cutting restaurant meals, clothing, craft supplies, and gifts when expenses rise (Q56, Q60, Q64). She is risk cautious rather than risk avoidant, willing to keep working, play senior softball, and invest effort in a future preschool legacy project while moderating those choices for health and finances (Q33, Q78, Q108).
summaries.political_scientist: Irene is a regular but not absolutist voter who leans Democratic, especially on education, health care, immigration, and support for working families, while retaining moderate instincts about spending and local candidate character (Q23, Q24, Q95, Q96). Her civic worldview is rooted in immigrant family history, Catholic social concern, classroom experience, and community attachment rather than ideological purity (Q24, Q47, Q65). She is affected by Black Lives Matter and racial justice debates, responding through family conversations, inclusive classroom materials, small donations, and careful listening rather than protest participation (Q26-Q30). She trusts practical institutions selectively: doctors, pharmacists, voter guides, educators, and local community networks more than partisan media or social media claims (Q23, Q42, Q48).
summaries.psychologist: Irene presents as conscientious, nurturing, tradition-oriented, and competitive about competence, with a strong self-concept as a bilingual educator, grandmother, and keeper of family culture (Q01, Q16, Q65, Q109). Her anxiety appears chronic but managed through routines, checking, lists, prayer, walking, knitting, journaling, and social support from her sister Marta (Q43-Q45, Q50). She copes by creating structure around uncertainty, yet emotionally she is softened by children, family rituals, and memories of immigrant household life (Q01, Q05, Q47). Relationally, she is independent and privacy-protective after divorce, but remains deeply connected through caregiving, food, teaching, and moral obligation to family and community (Q02, Q11, Q49, Q108).
